newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Airlines, unions optimistic after talks.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Airlines, unions optimistic after talks.

text.p: A meeting between Canadian Airlines Corp. and unions aimed at resolving differences on a plan to rescue the ailing carrier ended Wednesday with new optimism that agreements would be reached.
Union leaders said Canadian's management showed newfound flexibility during the Vancouver talks in its approach to averting the airline's financial failure.

"There is an apparent new joint commitment to get this airline up and flying in a stable and ongoing fashion for an extended period of time," said Neville Hamilton, spokesman for the 5,300-member International Association of Machinists.
Neither the six unions nor the company would offer specifics regarding new alternatives discussed on Wednesday.

But Hamilton said Canadian management recognized assertions from its biggest unions that the 10 percent employee wage cuts that were part of the three-pronged survival plan "will not work and they're definitely prepared to positively explore additional alternatives with us."
The parties agreed to take issues raised at the talks back to their staffs and meet again in the next week.

The airline's big unions, including the IAM and 3,700-member Canadian Auto Workers (CAW), have so far rejected its plans to cut employee wages and criticized its information meetings with thousands of employees the past two weeks.
The have also rejected an idea, supported by the company and the Canadian government, to allow members to vote freely on the survival strategy.

The IAM had launched a complaint with Canada's federal labor board over the carrier's employee sessions, but canceled a hearing on Tuesday and agreed to the meeting with Canadian Chief Executive Kevin Benson. Canadian, in turn, halted the information sessions.

Despite accepting Benson's invitation to talk, the CAW said it did not plan to change its call for the wage-cut rejection, government bailout of the airline and re-regulation of Canada's air industry.

"The positive thing for us is that they're talking to the union as opposed to going around threatening our members," CAW president Buzz Hargrove said in an interview after his staff met with Benson Wednesday.
"But it doesn't mean we're any more willing to give up our wages than we ever were -- we are not giving any 10 percent pay cut."

Benson has said the survival plan, which also includes route restructurings and a C$48 million ($36 million) cut in annual service fees, was not negotiable and that the company would wind up operations if all participants did not agree by a Nov. 30 deadline.
Some CAW employees in Calgary, frustrated by their union leadership, have begun circulating petitions for a free vote on the wage cut proposal.
But Hargrove said most workers, including those based in Toronto and Vancouver, supported the union leadership's view that 10 percent wage cuts were not a solution to Canadian's financial woes.
"Overall, we'll have an overwhelming vote here to reject this further cut," he said.
Meanwhile, no agreement had been reached by Wednesday between Canadian and AMR Corp., parent of American Airlines, on fee concessions, but intense talks were continuing, said AMR spokesman Al Becker.
Becker repeated, however, that AMR was not interested in infusing Canadian with cash by boosting its stake. AMR has a 33 percent stake in Canadian.
The IAM's Hamilton would not say if asking AMR to buy more of Canadian was one of the alternatives discussed on Wednesday.
